name: Images of Text
explanation: This criterion requires using real, styled text instead of an image that merely depicts text, whenever the same visual result can be achieved with actual text. An image of text is a picture — a screenshot, a graphic exported from a design tool, a scanned page — where words are baked into the pixels rather than rendered as characters. Real text can be resized, reflowed, recolored, and read by assistive technology using the user's own settings and preferences; an image of text is a fixed picture that ignores all of that. There are two narrow exceptions: a logo or brand name is allowed to be an image (its exact rendering IS the point), and situations where a particular visual presentation — such as a specific font used for a stylized effect — is essential to the information and can't be reproduced with CSS or a web font.
whoItAffects: People with low vision who increase browser zoom or apply custom font sizes to make text readable find that images of text stay a fixed size and become pixelated or blurry when magnified, while real text stays crisp and reflows cleanly. People with dyslexia or other reading disabilities who rely on a personal style sheet or browser extension to change font, spacing, or color for easier reading get no benefit from an image of text, because those overrides only affect real text, not pixels. Screen reader users depend on whatever alt text was written for the image, which is often missing, truncated, or a poor stand-in for reading the actual words. People with situational or fluctuating vision needs, like fatigue or bright-glare conditions, also benefit from being able to recolor or restyle text that would otherwise be locked into an image.

codeExample.good: Simple, Transparent Pricing

howToTest: Zoom the page to 200% (or use your browser's text-only zoom) and look for any text-like content that turns blurry, pixelated, or stays a fixed size while text around it reflows and stays sharp — that's a strong signal it's an image of text rather than real text. You can also try selecting the text with your cursor: real text highlights and can be copied, while an image of text cannot be selected at all. Right-click any suspicious element and check whether 'Save Image As' or 'Open image in new tab' appears — if it does, it's an image. Finally, check whether the element is a wordmark/logo (fine as an image) or ordinary content like a heading, button label, or paragraph (should be real text).

check.question: A marketing page uses a PNG screenshot of a headline styled in a decorative font, with alt text containing the headline words. Does this satisfy SC 1.4.5 Images of Text?
choices: Yes, because the alt text lets screen reader users access the words
No, because the same visual result could be achieved with real text and CSS/web fonts, and this isn't a logo
Yes, because any image with alt text is accessible by definition
It depends only on whether the image loads quickly enough
